lead: An LVDT (linear variable differential transformer) turns a small straight-line movement of a magnetic core into an AC voltage. At the centre the two secondary windings give equal voltages and the output is zero. Slide the core either way and one secondary gains while the other loses, so the difference is proportional to the distance moved, and its phase tells the direction. The core never touches the windings, so there is no wear and almost no friction. You will find LVDTs in machine tools, hydraulic valves, thickness gauges and pressure transmitters.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for mutual inductance and reluctance, and Unit 1 for linearity and sensitivity.

blocks.text: An LVDT is a transformer built on a hollow insulating tube called the former. One primary winding and two secondary windings sit on this tube. A rod of magnetic material, the core, slides inside the tube without touching it.

items: Former: an insulating cylinder, often fibreglass or epoxy, that holds the windings and lets the core move freely.
Primary winding: wound at the centre of the former and driven by an AC source.
Secondary windings S₁ and S₂: identical, wound symmetrically on either side of the primary, so a centred core links both equally.
Core: soft iron or nickel–iron with high permeability, fixed to the part whose movement is measured.
Shield: a magnetic shield of high-permeability alloy around the assembly, plus an earthed case, to reject stray fields and electrostatic pickup.

blocks.text: The two secondaries are connected in series opposition, so the terminals give the difference of their voltages. A drift in supply voltage or temperature hits both windings almost equally, and the difference cancels it. That is why the device is called differential, and why it is steadier than the single-coil variable-reluctance sensor of 3.1.

blocks.where: V₁ and V₂ are the rms voltages induced in S₁ and S₂, in volts; x is the core displacement from the centre position, in millimetres, positive toward S₁; K is the sensitivity in volts per millimetre at the excitation actually used. Datasheets often quote sensitivity per volt of excitation, S in mV/(mm·V); at an excitation of V_exc volts rms the constant is K = S × V_exc, in volts per millimetre.

sections.h3: How the output voltage is formed

blocks.text: The primary is excited from an AC source, usually a few volts rms at a frequency between about 1 kHz and 10 kHz. The primary current sets up a magnetic flux along the tube. The core, a good path for flux, carries that flux to the secondaries, and each secondary gets a voltage by mutual induction.

items: Hold the core exactly at the centre. Both secondaries link the same flux, so V₁ = V₂ and V_out = 0. This is the null position.
Move the core toward S₁. More flux passes through S₁ and less through S₂, so V₁ rises, V₂ falls, and V_out = V₁ − V₂ grows in phase with the excitation.
Move the core the other way. Now V₁ < V₂ and the difference swings 180° in phase; the magnitude is the same for the same distance, but the sign has flipped.
Feed the output to a phase-sensitive demodulator, which compares it with the excitation and produces a signed DC voltage.

blocks.text: Magnitude alone cannot separate the two sides of null, because a plain voltmeter reads the same on both. The phase carries the direction, and a demodulator recovers it (see Unit 6, Signal Conditioning, Data Acquisition and Actuators).
Displacement is then read from x = V_out / K. The relation holds only inside the linear range, roughly the middle portion of the core travel.

head: Characteristic
What it means
rows: Deviation of output from a straight line over the working range; commonly quoted as ±0.1 % to ±1 % of full-scale output.

Output per millimetre per volt of excitation, in mV/(mm·V). At an excitation of V_exc volts rms the constant in V_out = K·x is K = S × V_exc, in volts per millimetre. It rises with excitation voltage and with secondary turns.
The small output still present at null, caused by winding mismatch, harmonics and capacitive coupling. It is never zero, only a small fraction of full-scale output.
Core travel in each direction from null, from a fraction of a millimetre up to a few hundred millimetres.
How closely the same core position gives the same null on repeated visits, typically to a few micrometres.
Set by the readout electronics, not by the winding, because the core has no sliding contact, so there is no stiction and the output changes continuously with position.
Reverses by 180° as the core crosses null, so phase-sensitive demodulation is required.

blocks.text: The core floats, so friction and hysteresis are very low and the life is long. The moving mass of the core and the excitation frequency limit the dynamic response, so a light core and a higher carrier frequency give a faster sensor.

items: Displacement: direct measurement of valve lift, beam deflection or specimen extension, static or slowly varying.
Thickness: a roller rides on the sheet or foil and the core moves with the roller, so a change in thickness becomes a voltage. Used on paper, plastic film and metal strip.
Pressure: a Bourdon tube or diaphragm moves the core; pressure becomes displacement and then voltage (see 3.7 for how the sensing element itself is built).
Position feedback: servo systems, machine-tool slides, hydraulic spool position and aircraft control surfaces.
Why it is chosen: it measures static displacement, needs no contact, and gives a bipolar output that tells direction as well as size.

figure.caption: The signal path from excitation to a signed reading: the core position changes how much flux each secondary links, and the difference of the two secondary voltages is then demodulated so that phase becomes a sign.

examples.question: An LVDT is excited at 5 V rms. At a core position the secondary voltages are V₁ = 2.00 V rms and V₂ = 1.60 V rms. The sensitivity is 0.50 V/mm at that 5 V rms excitation. Find (a) the differential output, (b) the displacement, (c) the direction, (d) the output at null.
steps: Differential output: V_out = V₁ − V₂ = 2.00 − 1.60 = 0.40 V rms.
The constant K = 0.50 V/mm applies at the 5 V rms drive used here; the per-volt figure is S = 100 mV/(mm·V), and 100 mV/(mm·V) × 5 V = 0.50 V/mm.
V₁ is larger than V₂, so the core has moved toward S₁, the side whose secondary gained voltage. Direction: 0.80 mm toward S₁.
At null the core is centred, so V₁ = V₂ and V_out = 0 V rms ideally; a real unit leaves a few millivolts of residual voltage.
The same 0.40 V rms reading would appear at 0.80 mm on the S₂ side, but with opposite phase. Only the phase separates the two.
examples.answer: V_out = 0.40 V rms, displacement = 0.80 mm toward S₁, and the ideal null output is 0 V.
examples.check:
v1 = 2.00
v2 = 1.60
s = 0.50
v_out = round(v1 - v2, 2)
x = round(v_out / s, 2)
null_out = 0.0
print(v_out)
print(x)
print(null_out)

traps: Reading the AC magnitude alone as displacement. A plain voltmeter gives the same reading on both sides of null; the phase must be demodulated to get the sign.
Writing V_out = V₁ + V₂. The secondaries are in series opposition, so the output is the difference; the sum is what a wrongly wired unit gives, and it stays large even at null.
Assuming the output is zero at null in a real sensor. Residual voltage from winding mismatch and harmonics always leaves a small offset.
Using V_out = K·x beyond the linear range and expecting a straight line near the ends of core travel.
Forgetting the excitation level. A sensitivity quoted per volt of excitation must be multiplied by the actual drive voltage before it is used as K.

quiz.q: Where is the primary winding placed in an LVDT, and how are the two secondaries connected?
quiz.a: The primary sits at the centre of the former, with two identical secondaries wound symmetrically on either side. The secondaries are connected in series opposition so the output is V₁ − V₂.

quiz.q: Explain why the LVDT output is zero at the null position.
quiz.a: At null the high-permeability core is centred, so it links both identical secondaries with the same flux. Mutual induction then gives V₁ = V₂, and their difference V₁ − V₂ is zero.

quiz.q: Why does a simple AC voltmeter fail to show the direction of core movement?
quiz.a: A voltmeter shows only magnitude. Moving 0.8 mm to either side of null gives the same |V₁ − V₂|; the two cases differ only by a 180° phase reversal, which needs a phase-sensitive demodulator to detect.

quiz.q: An LVDT has sensitivity 0.80 V/mm at 4 V rms excitation. It gives V₁ = 1.50 V rms and V₂ = 1.90 V rms. Find the output and the displacement, with direction.
quiz.a: V_out = 1.90 − 1.50 = 0.40 V rms in magnitude, with V₂ larger, so the core is toward S₂. x = 0.40 / 0.80 = 0.50 mm toward S₂.

quiz.q: A thickness gauge uses an LVDT of sensitivity 2.0 V/mm at its rated excitation. The sheet thickness changes by 0.05 mm and the core follows the roller. What output change appears, in mV?
A student tests an LVDT and finds a small but non-zero reading with the core visibly centred. Give two causes and state whether the linearity claim is affected.
quiz.a: The reading is the residual voltage, caused by mismatched secondary windings and by capacitive coupling plus harmonics in the excitation. It is an offset at null, not a slope error, so sensitivity and linearity over the range can still be good; the offset should be measured and subtracted, or trimmed in the demodulator.

quiz.q: An LVDT pressure transmitter gives a full-scale output at the rated pressure, but the reading saturates early. Suggest the likely cause and one check.
quiz.a: The pressure-driven element (Bourdon tube or diaphragm) has pushed the core past the linear range, where the output flattens. Check the core travel against the quoted range and rescale the linkage so full-scale pressure keeps the core well inside it; also confirm the demodulator is not clipping.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial LVDTs often come as a complete transducer with the demodulator inside the housing, giving 0–10 V or 4–20 mA for a PLC. An AC-excited LVDT suits hot or radioactive zones where electronics would fail, because only the windings and core sit there. Printed-coil variants make thin sensors for micro-positioning and MEMS. Search for LVDT signal conditioner ICs, half-bridge and RVDT variants, and LVDT calibration.
